Ophir
ō'fēr
n. (a land famous for the finest gold, reached by Solomon's navy from Eziongeber; also a son of Joktan in the table of nations)
From Hebrew 'Ophir, of uncertain meaning, first the name of a man — the eleventh son of Joktan (Gen 10:29) — and afterward of the country his descendants settled. In Scripture the word finally becomes a byword for quality: gold of Ophir is the Hebrew way of saying the best gold there is.

Biblical Definition

Ophir enters as a name in the table of nations, “And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan” (Gen 10:29), and leaves as a proverb. The trade began with Solomon and Hiram of Tyre: “And they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to king Solomon” (1Ki 9:28), and the same fleet brought “great plenty of almug trees, and precious stones” (1Ki 10:11). The voyage was long — three years out and back — and it required a harbour on the Red Sea, which is why Jehoshaphat's later attempt to revive it failed before it sailed: “Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Eziongeber” (1Ki 22:48). Where Ophir lay is not stated and cannot now be settled — Arabia, east Africa and India have all been argued. What Scripture cares about is the standard the name became. Job weighs wisdom against it: “It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire” (Job 28:16). The psalmist dresses the king's bride in it: “upon thy right hand did stand the queen in gold of Ophir” (Psa 45:9). Isaiah makes it the measure of how scarce men will be in the day of the LORD's anger: “I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir” (Isa 13:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Ophir; in sacred history it is a country famous for gold, whither the navy of Solomon sailed from Eziongeber.

expand to see more

OPHIR, n. A son of Joktan, and the country peopled by his posterity.

A land renowned for gold, and for almug trees and precious stones.

Solomon's navy, with the servants of Hiram, fetched thence four hundred and twenty talents of gold.

Jehoshaphat afterward made ships to go to Ophir, but they were broken at Eziongeber.

The gold of Ophir is used in Scripture as the proverbial standard of the finest gold.

Key Scripture

1Ki 9:28 — "And they came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold, four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to king Solomon."

1Ki 22:48 — "Jehoshaphat made ships of Tharshish to go to Ophir for gold: but they went not; for the ships were broken at Eziongeber."

Job 28:16 — "It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir, with the precious onyx, or the sapphire."

Isa 13:12 — "I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this place. The principle to recover is that Scripture uses the world's highest valuation only to be outbid — wisdom, a man, and the knowledge of God are each priced above the gold of Ophir.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Ophir is a gold country whose site is unknown and nobody has contested it. What the name does in Scripture is provide a fixed point of value against which better things are measured. Job 28 is the classic passage: the chapter surveys the whole mining industry of the ancient world, men cutting shafts into the rock and turning up the earth as by fire, and then asks where wisdom shall be found — and answers that it cannot be got for gold, nor weighed against the gold of Ophir, and that “the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28:28).

The principle to recover is that the Bible does not despise wealth in order to make its point; it uses wealth as a real measure and then names something that outweighs it. Peter writes of a faith “much more precious than of gold that perisheth” (1Pe 1:7), and Christ counsels the Laodiceans to buy of Him “gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich” (Rev 3:18). A ministry that can only denounce riches has not learned this language. The Bible names the best the world can offer, grants that it is genuinely good, and then sets it in the scale against the fear of the LORD and watches the balance move.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Ophir (H211), Ophir; zahab (H2091), gold; kethem (H3800), pure or fine gold; 'oniy (H590), fleet, navy of ships; 'almuggiym (H484), almug trees.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Ophir (H211) — Ophir; a son of Joktan and the land of his seed.

Hebrew zahab (H2091) — gold; the commodity that made the name.

Hebrew kethem (H3800) — fine gold; the word in ‘gold of Ophir’ at Job 28:16.

Hebrew 'oniy (H590) — navy, fleet; Solomon's ships out of Eziongeber.

Hebrew 'almuggiym (H484) — almug wood; brought home with the gold.

Usage

"“They came to Ophir, and fetched from thence gold” — the voyage that made a kingdom rich."

"“It cannot be valued with the gold of Ophir” — wisdom outbidding the best market rate."

"“The queen in gold of Ophir” — the bride of the King arrayed in the finest there is."
